title: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse, while Jinjiang's grassroots shoe factories ran ahead
dek: Li Honggu says Li Ning is a company made of countless mismatches: its founder had no ambition for business, held resources no one could match, and those resources became a curse instead. Jinjiang's shoe factories were started by Minnan farmers pooling household funds, carried no baggage, and made decisions purely around the market — and over the long run they ran more steadily.
why: The industry-history section lays out rare mechanisms like joint-household fundraising, "kill the pests, protect the flowers," and the half-mountain theory; the second half has Li Honggu dissecting why Li Ning was overtaken and how capital became the new curse — the sharpest part.
who: Founders and investors in consumer brands, manufacturing, or family-business governance; anyone who wants to know why Li Ning and Anta took different paths.
skip: The Ding clan ancestral hall observations from 9:58 are more anecdote — fast-forward to the Nike contract-manufacturing line at 15:58.

points.h: Jinjiang is not the Fujian version of the Wenzhou model
points.body: Fei Xiaotong summed up Chinese rural development into four models: Sunan had government leading farmers to start factories, Wenzhou relied on individual entrepreneurs, the Pearl River Delta relied on foreign capital plus labor for processing-and-assembly. Jinjiang appeared last and is the easiest to underestimate. It was not individual entrepreneurs but township enterprises started by several families and relatives pooling funds, with a quasi-private shareholding character: in 1979, when Lin Tuqin started Jinjiang's first shoe factory, he gathered 14 village households to buy in — these people were both shareholders and employees; in 1982, when they wanted to strike out on their own, they also split from the original factory into five factories. The money came from the Minnan-specific biao hui, sitting in a gray zone of finance, and many companies that later grew big raised their early money this way. The local government also proposed the "five allowances": allowing dividends, share-based fundraising, hired labor, and sales commissions.

points.h: Under the fake-medicine case, the government chose to kill the pests and protect the flowers
points.body: Jinjiang had two early quality crises. One was "week shoes" and "street-crossing shoes": farmers didn't understand that shoes needed specialized glue, and used ordinary glue to stick soles to uppers, so they came apart after seven days — one consumer said they came apart just crossing the street. The second was the 1985 fake-medicine case: white sugar ground into powder, congealed into blocks, stuffed with white fungus to pass as granules, flowing through gray channels to hospitals, reported nationally by People's Daily. Jinjiang goods became notorious, over a thousand ground-promotion salespeople were turned away, and some hotels threw their luggage out the door. At the time, Fujian's first provincial party secretary, Xiang Nan, was very market-oriented — he expanded the Xiamen special economic zone, borrowed international loans to build Xiamen airport, and called Chendai's workshops "a flower of township enterprises" — yet for this he was criticized as too far to the left, made five or six self-criticisms within half a year, and then stepped down. On his way out he instructed the people handling the fake-medicine case: kill the pests and protect the flowers; when you pour out the bathwater, don't throw the baby out with it.

points.h: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse instead
points.body: Jinjiang's shoe factories were all Nike's apprentices, but the first to develop the awareness of building a domestic brand was Li Ning. Li Ning founded its brand in 1990, collecting a sacred flame beneath the snow mountains of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and passing it nationwide, with enormous impact; the registration milestones of Jinjiang brands almost all come after this — Anta applied in 1990 and registered successfully in 1991, Peak was originally named Fengdeng and changed its name in 1990-1991, and 361° was previously called Bieke. But the two paths were completely different: Li Ning carried a national halo from its founding, and when performance doubled year after year in the mid-1990s it set the goal of spending ten or twenty years to put a Chinese brand in the world's number one position; its founder had no ambition for business and hired professional managers to run it, and it fell into crisis and internal friction again and again. Jinjiang brands were grassroots, carried no historical baggage, and made every decision around the market.

points.h: The family that gave away 51% hit every node right
points.body: In 1988, Ding Shizhong was not yet 18, had dropped out of middle school, and persuaded his father to give him 10,000 yuan to buy 600 to 700 pairs of shoes; he rode a hard seat for two days and two nights to Beijing and became one of the first Beijing drifters. Around the same time, Li Ning was wearing Li Ning-brand clothes carrying the Asian Games sacred flame in Beijing. He wanted to sell Jinjiang shoes into Xidan and Wangfujing, but those were powerful state-run department stores, and a 17- or 18-year-old kid from Fujian simply couldn't get in; it took him one or two years of grinding before he got a counter. Another easily overlooked point is his father, Ding Hemu: the only male heir in the family, his family was actually weak in the village — Minnan clans fought over land and factory buildings, relying on having many sons and on fists, and Ding Hemu didn't participate. He taught his son to give others more benefit in doing business: "give others 51% of the benefit, keep only 49% for yourself."

points.h: Inventory enough for the whole nation to wear for three years
points.body: Around 2000, Anta signed Kong Linghui and advertised on CCTV and became an overnight sensation; on top of the Sydney Olympics, the men's football team reaching the World Cup, and the successful Olympic bid, the whole industry frantically signed spokespeople and opened stores, with the peak year opening close to 1,000 stores. Peak founder Xu Jingnan's metaphor was "riding an elevator": a person standing still in the elevator still grows, and everyone thought that after the Beijing Olympics they would ride an even faster elevator. But two or three years after the Olympics the inventory crisis erupted: one manager described it as, even if Jinjiang's shoe factories stopped producing, the shoes in inventory would be enough for the whole Chinese population to wear for three years. The root cause was the distribution model of feudalism plus a futures system — ordering half a year in advance, the brand too far from the market, and distributors unwilling to share real sales data. Anta's response was to strengthen centralization; Ding Shizhong personally toured stores like an emperor on campaign, and in the worst one or two years walked 400 to 500-plus market points in China.

points.h: The book is missing Nike and Adidas as the coordinate system
points.body: Li Honggu's biggest criticism of the book is that it lacks an implicit thread: Nike and Adidas's campaigns in the Chinese market actually determined the rises and falls of Chinese brands to a greater extent — they are the real coordinates. Huang Ziyi agrees, but explains that there is too little detailed material on Adidas and Nike's playbook, because multinational companies have to go through procedures and have discipline when giving interviews. Li Honggu also argues that Li Ning's problems cannot be explained by the professional-manager system: Li Ning is "a company made of countless mismatches" — he was not happy doing business, his resource endowment far exceeded everyone else's, yet it formed a huge gap with his vision and strategy, and the resources became a curse instead. And today, after Jinjiang brands obtained capital and acquired international brands, a new problem has appeared: how to tell a story of an international brand with yourself — "capital became their curse."

points.h: Anta's multi-brand: independent front end, shared middle and back office
points.body: Anta's doing FILA was learned. Li Ning was first overtaken by Nike in 2003 and lost its market number one, and was the earliest to try multi-brand; Li Ning's first professional manager, Chen Yihong, also did KAPPA very well. When Anta acquired FILA, it initially also slapped FILA labels on traditional Anta products, and only after they didn't sell did it painfully start over: in organizational structure and process, keep the FILA team absolutely independent from the Anta team, prevent mutual influence, then poach a world-class team for design, move toward fashion and trends, and do DTC direct retail at the same time. Once it worked, Anta's multi-brand mechanism was: the retail end and the product design and R&D end each independent, sharing Anta's powerful middle and back office, including human resources, the contract-manufacturing system, and Jinjiang's industrial cluster. What Ding Shizhong now repeatedly says is: I don't want to make China's Nike, what I want to make is the world's Anta.

points.h: Once per-capita GDP passes $10,000, verticals take off
points.body: When Huang Ziyi interviewed Anta in 2021, an Anta vice president explained why it acquired Amer Sports, Descente, and Kolon: based on their research in European and American markets, when a country's per-capita GDP reaches $10,000, niche sports tracks begin to emerge — ice and snow, outdoor, hiking; when it reaches $20,000, these niche sports begin to flourish on a large scale. At the time of the interview China had just crossed $10,000, and now Beijing and Shanghai have already exceeded $20,000, with the national average around $15,000, so these brands taking off may be a natural process. Where Anta is stronger than others is that it may, through a relatively advanced professional-manager consciousness, be first to do market research and lock up these tracks.

Mutual-aid lending in Minnan's acquaintance society, sitting in a gray zone of finance, and the startup funding source for early factories.
The policy proposed by Chendai and Jinjiang local governments: allow dividends, allow share-based fundraising, allow hired labor, allow sales commissions.

The brand itself opens stores and deals directly with consumers, bypassing layer upon layer of distributors.
